'''Robert M. Wald''' ({{IPAc-en|w|ɔː|l|d}}; born  June 29, 1947, in [[New York City]]) is an American [[theoretical physics|theoretical]] [[physicist]] and professor at the [[University of Chicago]]. He studies general relativity, black holes, and [[quantum gravity]] and has written textbooks on these subjects.

== Life and education ==
He is the son of the mathematician and statistician [[Abraham Wald]] and great-grandson of the chief rabbi [[Moshe Shmuel Glasner]]. Wald's parents died in a plane crash when he was three years old.<ref name="Morgenstern1951">{{cite journal
 | doi = 10.2307/1907462
 | author = Morgenstern, Oskar
 | author-link = Oskar Morgenstern
 | journal = Econometrica
 | volume = 19
 | issue = 4
 | pages = 361–367
 | year = 1951
 | title = Abraham Wald, 1902–1950
 | publisher = Econometrica, Vol. 19, No. 4
 | jstor = 1907462
}}</ref> He earned his bachelor's degree from Columbia University in 1968 and his PhD in physics from Princeton University in 1972,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Alumni Sons and Daughters {{!}} Columbia College Today|url=https://www.college.columbia.edu/cct/archive/sep_oct08/alumni_profiles7|access-date=January 18, 2022|website=Columbia College Today|archive-date=October 30, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221030110640/https://www.college.columbia.edu/cct/archive/sep_oct08/alumni_profiles7|url-status=dead}}</ref> under the supervision of [[John Archibald Wheeler]]. His doctoral dissertation was titled ''Nonspherical Gravitational Collapse and Black Hole Uniqueness''.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11610033.html|title=Robert M. Wald|website=American Institute of Physics|access-date=July 18, 2019}}</ref>

== Career and contributions ==
Between 1972 and 1974, Robert Wald worked as a research associate in physics at the [[University of Maryland, College Park|University of Maryland]].<ref name=":1" /> He then moved to the University of Chicago, spending two years as a postdoctoral fellow before joining the faculty in 1976.<ref name=":2" /> He wanted to move to Chicago in order to work with [[Robert Geroch]] and other specialists in gravitation.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book|title=S. Chandrasekhar - The Man Behind the Legend|publisher=Imperial College Press|year=1997|isbn=1-86094-038-2|editor-last=Wali|editor-first=Kameshwar C.|location=Singapore|pages=[https://archive.org/details/schandrasekharma0000unse/page/80 80–85]|chapter=13. Some Memories of Chandra - Robert M. Wald|chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/schandrasekharma0000unse/page/80}}</ref>

In 1977, Wald published a popular-science book titled ''Space, Time, and Gravity: The Theory of the Big Bang and Black Holes'' explaining Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity, and its implications in cosmology and astrophysics. The book also gives a survey of what was then ongoing research on [[gravitational collapse]] and [[black hole]]s. This book grew out of a series of lectures Wald gave as part of the Compton Lectures at the University of Chicago in the spring of 1976.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Moché, Dinah L.|author-link1=Dinah L. Moché|date=May 1978|title=Review of ''Space, Time, and Gravity'' by Robert M. Wald|journal=Physics Teacher|volume=16|issue=5|page=332|doi=10.1119/1.2339970}}</ref> The Compton Lectures, given every Spring and Fall quarter, are intended to explain notable advances in the physical sciences to members of the general public.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://efi.uchicago.edu/page/compton-lectures|title=Arthur H. Compton Lectures|publisher=Enrico Fermi Institute, University of Chicago|access-date=July 19, 2019}}</ref>

He published the textbook ''[[General Relativity (book)|General Relativity]]'' in 1984. Aimed at beginning graduate students, it covers [[spinor]]s, the [[variational principle]]s, the [[Initial value formulation (general relativity)|initial-value formulation]], (exact) gravitational waves, singularities, [[Penrose diagram]]s, [[Hawking radiation]], and [[Black hole thermodynamics|black-hole thermodynamics]].<ref>[https://math.ucr.edu/home/baez/physics/Administrivia/rel_booklist.html#intro_gr A Guide to Relativity Books]. [[John C. Baez]] et al. University of California, Riverside. September 1998. Accessed January 18, 2019.</ref> It is well-received,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Smolin |first=Lee |author-link=Lee Smolin |date=January–February 1986 |title=Review: ''General Relativity'' by Robert Wald |journal=American Scientist |volume=74 |issue=1 |page=82 |jstor=27853954}}</ref><ref name=":20">{{Cite book |last=Feynman |first=Richard |title=Feynman Lectures on Gravitations |last2=Morinigo |first2=Fernando B. |last3=Wagner |first3=William G. |publisher=Westview |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-813-34038-8 |editor-last=Hatfield |editor-first=Brian |location=Boulder, Colorado |chapter=Preface by John Preskill and Kip Thorne |chapter-url=http://www.theory.caltech.edu/~preskill/pubs/preskill-1995-feynman.pdf}}</ref> but has become outdated by the early twenty-first century.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Finley |first=Daniel |date=April 1, 2018 |title=A List of Technical Books on General Relativity |url=https://physics-old.unm.edu/Courses/Finley/p581/Booklist.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240320103950/https://physics.unm.edu/Courses/Finley/p581/Booklist.html |archive-date=March 20, 2024 |access-date=December 23, 2025 |website= |publisher=Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of New Mexico |url-status=live }}</ref>

Wald has taught first-year graduate courses covering a broad range of topics, including classical mechanics, quantum mechanics, statistical mechanics, and electromagnetism. He has also taught courses on [[general relativity]], his specialty, at both introductory and advanced levels. A particularly effective teacher, he received the Graduate Teaching Award from the University of Chicago in 1997.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal|last=Steele|first=Diana|title=Graduate Teaching Award: Robert Wald|journal=University of Chicago Chronicle|date=June 12, 1997|volume=16|issue=9|url=https://chronicle.uchicago.edu/970612/wald.shtml|accessdate=20 May 2013}}</ref>

Wald investigates black holes and their thermodynamics, and gravitational radiation-reaction (or self-force).<ref name=":2" /> During the early 1970s, Wald and a number of other theoretical physicists studied the external [[electric field]] lines of black holes,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cohen |first=Jeffrey |last2=Wald |first2=Robert |date=1971 |title=Point Charge in the Vicinity of a Schwarzschild Black Hole |url=https://pubs.aip.org/aip/jmp/article-abstract/12/9/1845/223700/Point-Charge-in-the-Vicinity-of-a-Schwarzschild?redirectedFrom=fulltext |journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics |volume=12 |pages=1845–1849 |doi=10.1063/1.1665812|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":9">{{Cite book |last=Thorne |first=Kip |author-link=Kip Thorne |title=Black Holes and Time Warps: Einstein's Outrageous Legacy |title-link=Black Holes and Time Warps |publisher=W. W. Norton & Company |year=1994 |isbn=0-393-03505-0 |location=New York}}</ref>{{Reference page|pages=407-8}} and subsequently the perturbations of black holes,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wald |first=Robert |date=1973 |title=On perturbations of a Kerr black hole |url=https://pubs.aip.org/aip/jmp/article-abstract/14/10/1453/223998/On-perturbations-of-a-Kerr-black-hole?redirectedFrom=fulltext |journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics |volume=14 |pages=1453–1461 |doi=10.1063/1.1666203|url-access=subscription }}</ref> following the publication of the Teukolsky equations by [[Saul Teukolsky]] in 1972.<ref name=":9" />{{Reference page|page=298}} Wald has published over 100 research papers on general relativity and [[quantum field theory in curved spacetime]], many of which have been cited by hundreds of subsequent papers.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://inspirehep.net/search?p=author%3AR.M.Wald.1%20AND%20collection%3Aciteable|title=Robert M. Wald|website=INSPIRE - HEP|access-date=August 16, 2019}}</ref> In 1993, he described the Wald entropy of a [[black hole]], which is dependent simply on the area of the event horizon of the black hole.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Black Hole Entropy is Noether Charge|journal = Physical Review D|volume = 48|issue = 8|pages = R3427–R3431|arxiv = gr-qc/9307038|doi = 10.1103/PhysRevD.48.R3427|year = 1993|last1 = Wald|first1 = Robert M.|pmid = 10016675|bibcode = 1993PhRvD..48.3427W|s2cid = 18398147}}</ref>

He organized The Symposium on Black Holes and Relativistic Stars in 1996, in honor of the late Nobel Prize-winning theoretical astrophysicist [[Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar]]. Distinguished speakers of this event included [[Stephen Hawking]], [[Roger Penrose]] and [[Martin Rees]]. Although the event charged an entrance fee of $100, Wald made sure all University of Chicago students were admitted free of charge.<ref name=":0" /> Chandrasekhar founded a research group on general relativity at the University of Chicago, which includes Wald, [[James Hartle]] and Robert Geroch.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://physics.uchicago.edu/about/our-history/|title=Our History. Chapter One: 1893 to 1986|last=Witten|first=Thomas|date=April 2018|publisher=Department of Physics, University of Chicago|access-date=July 19, 2019}}</ref> Although Wald and Chandrasekhar never collaborated on any particular research projects, the two developed warm relations.<ref name=":3" />

He became a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] (APS) in 1996<ref name=":1" /> and a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 2001.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2001 |title=Robert M. Wald |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/robert-m-wald-prubqc/ |access-date=August 16, 2019 |website=Member Directory |publisher=National Academy of Sciences}}</ref> He received the [[Einstein Prize (APS)|Einstein Prize]] from the APS Division of Gravitational Physics in 2017 for "the discovery of the general formula for black hole entropy, and for developing a rigorous formulation of quantum field theory in curved spacetime."<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/units/dgrav/awards/recipient.cfm?first_nm=Robert&last_nm=Wald&year=2017|title=2017 Einstein Prize Recipient|publisher=Division of Gravitational Physics, American Physical Society (APS)|access-date=July 18, 2019}}</ref>

Wald delivered a public lecture at the [[University of Alabama]] on October 27, 2015, titled "The Formulation of General Relativity," celebrating the centennial of Einstein's theory.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://physics.ua.edu/recent-events/gr-100-celebrating-the-centennial-of-einsteins-theory-of-general-relativity/|title=GR 100: Celebrating the Centennial of Einstein's Theory of General Relativity|publisher=Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Alabama|access-date=July 18, 2019}}</ref> Wald is a member of the [[LIGO]] group at the University of Chicago, headed by astrophysicist [[Daniel Holz]]. The Laser Interferometry Gravitational-wave Observatory detected [[gravitational wave]]s for the first time in 2015, one century after Einstein predicted their existence.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://news.uchicago.edu/story/ligo-detects-colliding-black-holes-third-time|title=LIGO detects colliding black holes for third time|date=July 1, 2017|work=UChicago News|access-date=July 19, 2019}}</ref>

In 2025 he received the [[Albert Einstein Medal]] from the [[Albert Einstein Society]] in Switzerland for his studies of classical and semi-classical gravity.<ref>{{Cite news |date=February 13, 2025 |title=Robert Wald awarded 2025 Albert Einstein Medal |url=https://physicalsciences.uchicago.edu/news/article/robert-wald-awarded-2025-albert-einstein-medal/ |publisher=Physical Sciences Division, University of Chicago}}</ref> In the same year, Wald, [[Gary Gibbons]], [[Gary Horowitz]], and [[Roy Kerr]] were awarded the [[Dirac Medal (ICTP)|Dirac Medal]] from the [[International Centre for Theoretical Physics|International Center for Theoretical Physics]] in Italy for their landmark contributions to the study of gravity, in both the classical and quantum regimes.<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 8, 2025 |title=2025 ICTP Dirac Medal Goes to Gravity Explorers {{!}} ICTP |url=https://www.ictp.it/news/2025/8/2025-ictp-dirac-medal-goes-gravity-explorers |access-date=January 2, 2026 |website=International Centre for Theoretical Physics}}</ref>
